title: Lift the dropper's arguments
briefing: auditd logs every program started on this host, with its arguments, as `key="value"` pairs in `var/log/audit/audit.log`. The dropper you found in Level 1 was started with a command line, and the command line names where it was sending its work.
Pull the program and its `--pool` value out of the record with one `sed` command: no grep, no hand copying.

lesson.p: `sed` edits a stream line by line. The command you will use most is `s/REGEX/REPLACEMENT/`. With `-n` sed prints nothing unless told to, and the `p` flag prints a line after a successful substitution. Together, `sed -n 's/.../.../p'` means: rewrite the matching lines, print only those, and drop the rest.

flags: replace the first match on each line; add `g` to replace every match
print only the lines you ask for. `sed -n '/RE/p'` works like grep.
extended regex: `( ) + ? |` without backslashes. Without -E write `\( \)`.
in the replacement: the text the first and second `( )` groups captured
any run of characters that are not a double quote: the value inside `key="..."`
an address range: print from the first line matching START through the next line matching END
line-number addresses: lines 2-4 / the last line
edit a file in place. Never run it on evidence; write to a new file instead.

lesson.note: `.*` is greedy: it matches as much as it can. In `s/.*a0="\([^"]*\)".*/\1/`, the leading `.*` eats everything up to the LAST `a0="` on the line. Use `[^"]*` instead of `.*` inside quotes, so the match stops at the closing quote.

Without `-n`, sed prints every line, changed or not, so a substitution on its own is an edit, not a filter. Adding `-n` and the `p` flag turns it into both: only the lines where the substitution matched come out, already rewritten.

examples.title: sed as grep

stages.why: Turn off sed's default of printing every line.
For lines that match, print. Same result as `grep 'Invalid user'`.

examples.output:
Mar 13 09:11:15 web-01 sshd[2140]: Invalid user admin from 203.0.113.9 port 40001
Mar 13 09:11:24 web-01 sshd[2145]: Invalid user test from 203.0.113.9 port 40013

examples.title: An address range: from one event to another

stages.why: Start at the first line that matches 09:11:15 and stop after the first line that matches 09:12:02.
Print the whole window: the brute-force attempts and the sudo line that follows them. Ranges are how you cut a time window out of a log.

Mar 13 09:11:15 web-01 sshd[2140]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.9 port 40001 ssh2

stages.why: Group 1: the IP, everything up to the first space.
Group 2: the method after the opening quote. Group 3: the path, up to the next space.
Replace the whole line with just the three groups.
The source address: digits and dots after `SRC=`.
Skip ahead to the destination port. The key names anchor the match, so it works whatever sits between them.
An IPv4 address. The first three octets are captured; the last one is not.
Keep the network, mask the host, on every address in the line (`g`). Logs often go into tickets or vendor cases, so trim them before they leave the team.

challenge.question: In var/log/audit/audit.log, the dropper's EXECVE record shows the program (a0) and the value that follows --pool (a2). Using sed, print both on one line.
challenge.format: The program path, one space, then the pool value, for example /usr/bin/foo 192.0.2.1:9999

hints: Look at the record first: `grep -- --pool var/log/audit/audit.log`. The values you want sit inside `a0="..."` and `a2="..."`, and `a1="--pool"` is what tells this line apart from the others.
Use `sed -n 's/.../\1 \2/p'`. Capture each value with `\([^"]*\)` (or `([^"]*)` with -E), and include the literal `a1="--pool"` between them so only this record matches.

why: The pool is the attacker's own address, 203.0.113.66, on port 4444. The dropper was not talking to a public mining pool; it reported back to the same machine that scanned and brute-forced this host. That port is your lead for the firewall log.

auditd only records programs if a rule asks for it. The `key="exec"` on the SYSCALL lines comes from a rule like `-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -k exec` in `/etc/audit/rules.d/`. On RHEL, `ausearch -k exec -i` decodes these records (including hex-encoded arguments) for you; sed is what you use when you only have the raw file.
When an argument contains a space or a quote, auditd writes it as hex instead (`a1=2D2D706F6F6C`), and your sed pattern finds nothing. `ausearch -i` or `xxd -r -p` turns it back into text.
